the prevalence of compulsive behaviours in PD was 67.4 % according to patients’ QUIPs and 66.6 % according to their carers’.
patients with PD and their carers tend to agree on the presence of IBC, but when they don’t, patients tend to underestimate the severity of the ICB, while carers tend to overestimate it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the agreement between patients and caregivers in reporting the presence and the severity of ICB in Parkinson’s disease.
the evaluation of the patients’ and their caregivers’ agreement in reporting ICB.
the comparison between patients and their carer’s perceptions about the presence of impulsive compulsive behaviours.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the agreement between the patient and his/her caregiver in referring the presence and severity of ICB is moderate.
patients and carers agree on the presence of IBDs in PD, but they do not agree in reporting the specific sub-items of ICDs and they do not agree on the severity of the ICB.
the degree of agreement between patients and their carer in reporting ICB is moderate, but it is lower in the presence of compulsivity in eating and hobbyism/punding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the agreement between patients and their carer in reporting the presence ICB is poor and the degree of agreement varies for each sub-item of the QUIP scale.
the agreement between patients and carers in reporting the presence and the type of ICB is moderate.
the agreement between patients’ and caregivers’ QUIPs is poor and the disagreement is mainly related to compulsive eating and hobbyism/punding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patients tend to underestimate their ICB, whereas their carers tend to overestimate them.

the agreement between patients and caregivers is poor in reporting ICB in PD.
